sources.citation: Thorvaldsdottir, Gudny Bjork. 2010. The Beginnings of Phonetic and Phonological Coding in the Signs of Ireland Digital Corpus: the Representation of Handshapes. The ITB Journal 11(1), Article 4, 13 pp. doi:10.21427/D7316R
sources.note: Handshape coding scheme for the Signs of Ireland corpus; zero hits for stress or prosody.

sources.citation: TEANGA 16 (1996), incl. McDonnell, Patrick, 'How Snowmen Move: Some Aspects of Lexical Choice in ISL' and Matthews, Patrick A., 'Extending the Lexicon of ISL' (ERIC ED414745)
sources.note: All 'stress' hits are in an unrelated article on English poetry; the two ISL papers are lexical.

sources.citation: Leeson, Lorraine & Irene Murtagh. 2020. Foreword. TEANGA Special Issue 11: iii-xiii. doi:10.35903/teanga.v11i.562
sources.note: Survey of ISL research to 2020; cites Thorvaldsdottir 2013 MA (ITB) 'Phonetic and Phonological Coding of ISL in the Signs of Ireland Corpus' and Leeson & Saeed 2012 as the volume-length description. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Murtagh, Irene. 2020. The Special Nature of Verbs in Sign Languages: An RRG Account of Irish Sign Language Verbs. TEANGA Special Issue 11. doi:10.35903/teanga.v11i1.204
sources.note: Computational phonological parameters (handshape, orientation, location, movement) of ISL verbs; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Smith, Robert G. & Markus Hofmann. 2020. A Lexical Frequency Analysis of Irish Sign Language. TEANGA Special Issue 11. doi:10.35903/teanga.v11i1.162; Leeson, Lorraine & John I. Saeed. 2020. Embodiment in Irish Sign Language Passives. TEANGA Special Issue 11. doi:10.35903/teanga.v11i.166
Fitzgerald, Angela. 2014. Mouthing and mouth gestures in Irish Sign Language: a Cognitive Linguistic framework. PhD thesis, Trinity College Dublin. 422 pp.http://hdl.handle.net/2262/80016
sources.note: 'Stress' only in the sense of emphasis: pp. 97-98 'Boyes-Braem states that mouthings add stress to the manual sign.. In the twelve Personal Stories examined here, we found six examples of repetition [of a mouthing] adding stress to the manual sign' (ISL example BAD NEGATIVE++). pp. 231-232 and 252 discuss prosody/intonation carried by non-manual features and body/torso spatial mapping, citing Wilcox, Sandler and Winston. No statement on word-level stress placement.

sources.citation: Mohr, Susanne. 2014. Chapter 2: The Linguistic Setup of Sign Languages – The Case of Irish Sign Language (ISL). In: Mouth Actions in Sign Languages: An Empirical Study of Irish Sign Language (Sign Languages and Deaf Communities 3), pp. 4-30. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. doi:10.1515/9781614514978.4 (open access, CC BY-NC-ND)
sources.note: Structural sketch of ISL (space, iconicity, simultaneity, non-manual features). p. 22: word stress and pitch are named as the only simultaneously ordered information in SPOKEN languages, contrasted with sign phonology which 'largely operates simultaneously'. p. 26: ISL non-manual features that change a sign's meaning are 'a pragmatic means comparable to the use of suprasegmentals and especially intonation in spoken languages' (WHO?/WHO!/'You are not who I think you are!', from Ó Baoill & Matthews 2000:174). No statement about word-level stress in ISL.

sources.citation: Leeson, Lorraine. 2001. Aspects of verbal valency in Irish Sign Language. PhD thesis, Trinity College Dublin. 339 pp.http://hdl.handle.net/2262/79586
sources.note: Four hits for 'stress', all in typological citations (Tomlin's word-order principles; Kiss 1995 'topic cannot bear the main stress of the sentence'; a glossed example FEEL MORE STRESS). Nothing about ISL stress or prosody beyond a note that topics are marked as intonational phrases (citing others).

sources.citation: McDonnell, Patrick. 1996. Verb categories in Irish Sign Language. PhD thesis, Trinity College Dublin. 392 pp.http://hdl.handle.net/2262/98532
sources.note: No stress/prosody statement; only a Brennan 1992 quotation on emphatic modifications 'stress[ing] the semantic content of the verb' and a bibliography entry (O'Halpin 1990 on contrastive stress in deaf children's speech).
